prize_parts.citation: For converting targeted protein degradation into a designable chemical principle, through heterobifunctional degraders that recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases and the cereblon-based molecular-glue mechanism

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B007, to Crews, Deshaies and Handa. The scientific core is that ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis becomes a designable chemical reaction in which a small molecule forms a ternary complex and the target protein is removed. After round 1, the claims that matter to me are measured ones. Independent groups have reproduced the degrader principle, ternary-complex structures and cooperativity measurements exist, and the cereblon mechanism is shown in patients by thalidomide-type drugs, which are glue degraders that are already approved. That last point answers the maturity objection more directly than the PROTAC drug pipeline does: the chemistry of induced proximity is clinically demonstrated, even if no heterobifunctional degrader is approved yet. Handa's identification of cereblon is the single decisive experiment that explains why those drugs work, so I keep him as the third name. The chair asks whether the citation should centre on PROTACs, glues or the concept. I think it should name the shared principle, induced proximity to an E3 ligase, with both mechanisms as its demonstrations. That gives a defensible set without Sakamoto, Gray, Ito, Kim and Ciulli, because the prize is for conceiving the principle and for explaining the glue branch. It is not a list of everyone who optimised ligands.
statement.case_against: The strongest objections stand. Crowded credit forces a cut that omits Ciulli, whose VHL ligands made PROTACs drug-like, as well as Sakamoto, Gray, Ito and Kim. A citation that covers both PROTACs and glues risks being read as two prizes under one heading, as Aili argues. No heterobifunctional degrader is approved, so a critic can still call the timing early. B061 has a cleaner single-laureate story and earlier patient data, and it commands wider explicit support in round 1 (four members against three for B007). I have not seen evidence that settles those points against B007, but I recognise that they are real.

responses.point: Brzezinski proposes a two-part prize of Crews and Deshaies for degraders and Liu for base editing, dropping Ciulli and Handa so that the configuration fits in three names.
responses.response: This is the only configuration that joins the two most supported ballots, and I take it seriously. My difficulty is the cost: it removes the cereblon discovery, which is the only part of B007 that explains an existing clinical drug class, and it leaves a citation built on a concept whose first clinical proof is still pending. I would accept it as a second choice before accepting a prize that omits degraders. I do not move to it as my first choice, because a pairing should rest on a shared principle, not on adding two partially supported ballots. Your own argument that the parts act on proteins and nucleic acids is better than a bridge, but it is a classification, not a common mechanism.

responses.point: Aili credits Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli and argues that Ciulli's structure-guided VHL ligands and the ternary-complex and cooperativity work turned PROTACs into a design discipline, with cereblon as a separate lineage.
responses.response: I agree that the quantitative ternary-complex work is what makes this chemistry rather than pharmacology, and I would not object to Ciulli if the committee settles on PROTACs alone. The difference between us is the question the chair posed. Without cereblon, the citation does not explain thalidomide, lenalidomide and pomalidomide, which are the approved evidence that induced degradation works in patients. Cereblon was a single decisive discovery, whereas VHL ligand design was developed in parallel by several groups. If you can show that Handa's contribution is not part of the same principle, I would reconsider, but I think the opposite is the better reading.

responses.point: Aqvist prefers B061 for Liu alone, with clean attribution, a clear chemical idea and a clear distinction from the 2020 CRISPR nuclease prize.
responses.response: Your argument is the strongest competing case, and I ranked B061 as my first alternative. I accept that attribution is cleaner and that deaminase chemistry is concrete. My remaining concerns are priority and weight. Nishida and Kondo's concurrent cytidine-deaminase work is still unresolved, as you say yourself, and I do not think it can be settled by recollection. On clinical stage, I do not see B061 as clearly ahead of B007: base editing has first patients but unsettled long-term safety, while the glue branch of B007 has years of approved use. I would not call that decisive for either side.

responses.point: Linke pairs sequencing-by-synthesis (Balasubramanian and Klenerman) with Liu, and in the chair summary asks whether any pairing shares a common principle or exists only to bridge first choices.
responses.response: I think your question is the right test, and I cannot find a shared mechanism in B001 plus B061. 'Reading and rewriting DNA' is a good description, but it does not unify one chemistry. I also remain unsure that sequencing-by-synthesis is the chemistry committee's discovery: credit is divided among Balasubramanian, Klenerman, Rothberg, Ju and Mayer, and a three-name cut leaves out claimants whom a measurement-minded reader would find hard to rank. If the committee wants two parts, I would prefer B007 with B061 over either of the other pairs.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that a citation covering both heterobifunctional degraders and the cereblon glue mechanism is one principle, or two achievements that should not share a heading.
Handa versus Ciulli for the third place, and the omission of Sakamoto, Gray, Ito and Kim.
Whether the absence of an approved heterobifunctional degrader, and the unsettled long-term safety of base editing, should change the ranking of B007 against B061.
I rely on my recollection of the literature and have not verified priority details, including Nishida and Kondo's priority relative to Liu.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My research on dNTP pools and ribonucleotide reductase is not connected to the degrader, base-editing, sequencing or nanopore candidates, and I have no recorded collaboration with any credited person. I have read the other members' disclosures in round 1 and none changes this.
